questions.question: Explain the separation of powers and describe the two houses of Parliament.
questions.expected_answer: The separation of powers divides the state into three branches so that no branch has too much power: the legislature, Parliament, makes laws; the executive, the President and cabinet, carries them out; and the judiciary, the courts, interprets the laws and checks that the other branches obey the Constitution. Parliament has two houses: the National Assembly, with four hundred members elected every five years, and the National Council of Provinces, with ninety members, ten from each province.

questions.question: Describe how a bill becomes a law, and name two other jobs of Parliament.
questions.expected_answer: A bill, or proposed law, is usually drawn up by a government department. Committees study it, and the public can comment or speak at hearings. It is debated and voted on in the National Assembly and considered by the NCOP. If both houses pass it, the President signs it and it becomes an Act. Parliament also elects the President, keeps oversight of the government by questioning ministers and checking spending, and approves the national budget.

questions.question: What is the Constitution, and why is it called the supreme law?
questions.expected_answer: The Constitution is the set of basic rules for how South Africa is governed, what powers the government has and what rights people have. It was signed by Mandela at Sharpeville on the tenth of December 1996 and came into effect in 1997. It is the supreme law because any law or government action that goes against it is invalid and can be struck down by the courts. It includes a preamble, founding values such as dignity, equality and freedom, and the Bill of Rights.
